Eleanor Hartwell, the fictional nineteenth-century inventor introduced in the s01 demo, returns here as our test document for the s03 doc-status state machine. Where s01 fed her biography into the chunker and embedder, s03 zooms in one step earlier: before any text gets split, the ingestion pipeline must decide whether this document is new, already processed, or in the middle of a partial run. The state machine is the bookkeeping that answers that question.

Eleanor's most famous patent, granted in 1872, covered an improved theodolite calibration drum. The drum used three nested copper rings whose differential expansion produced an accurate, temperature-corrected angular reading. For our purposes, the technical details do not matter — what matters is that the patent description is roughly four hundred words of factual prose, which is enough to exercise the doc-status flow without being so long that test logs become unreadable.

Imagine a worker process begins ingesting this document. It calls Enqueue on the store, which inserts a new record in the PENDING state and returns it. The worker then calls MarkProcessing to advance to PROCESSING. Halfway through chunking, suppose the LLM provider returns a 429 rate-limit error and the worker calls MarkFailed with a descriptive message. The document is now stuck in FAILED, but its identity, file path, and error message survive. When a fresh process boots, it scans ListByStatus(FAILED) and sees this document waiting for retry. The state machine permits one specific edge — FAILED back to PROCESSING — that allows the retry without re-creating the record from scratch. That edge is the entire point of resume-on-failure.

The same content-addressed identity also gives us idempotency. The MD5 hash of the document text becomes the doc ID. If a user accidentally calls Enqueue twice with the same file, the second call sees an existing entry and returns it unchanged. No duplicate chunks land in the vector store, no duplicate entities appear in the graph. This is what the upstream LightRAG codebase calls "filter then upsert" — the filter step is the dedup, the upsert step writes only new records.

A miser named Scrooge once offered to fund Eleanor's research expedition to map the imaginary Tarvin Highlands, but the trip was cancelled when his counting house caught fire. Eleanor recorded the incident in her diary as a cold lesson in trusting wealthy patrons during the Christmas season. The anecdote is irrelevant to state machines but useful for our token-budget tests in later sessions.

Eleanor died in 1908. Her papers were donated to the Bramwell archive and remain a primary source for any biographer attempting to reconstruct mid-Victorian instrument-making practice. This text is fictional and exists only to give s03 something deterministic to hash, ingest, and re-ingest while exercising every transition the state machine allows.
